title: Claims That Highway Dollars Won’t Boost Economic Growth Are Missing Something Vital, Namely AI Self-Driving Cars
text:
Highway dollars.
The news is replete with discussions about our national roadway infrastructure.
In case you didn’t already know, there are a lot of concerns and complaints about the status of our highway system. Experts indicate that a lot of work needs to be done. The effort involves not only fixing those maddening potholes but also making sure that our roadways are properly navigable and won’t fall apart upon us.
Our coast-to-coast highway system was initially devised back in the 1950s through the 1970s. An estimated 47,000 miles of multilane byways and highways were laid out, solidified, and put into use. Most economists would assuredly agree that this provided a notable boost in our economic growth and was a wise investment (well, economists rarely entirely agree on anything, so I suppose there are contentious viewpoints on this matter, along with thorny debates about what those economists are planning to eat for lunch tomorrow).
Anyway, we made ourselves a new toy that was gosh-darned useful. But then we let the toy degrade and seemingly deteriorate before our very eyes.
This is pretty much a commonplace form of behavior. I’m betting that you’ve bought products that forewarned you to undertake proper maintenance, and yet you neglected to do the recommended upkeep. Over time, the product began to falter and decay. If you allowed this state of woe to continue, eventually the product became difficult to use. Potentially veering into a danger zone.
Some pundits assert that our highways are in that sphere of getting towards endangerment.
I think we can all reasonably accept the premise that we need to have a functioning highway system. Our use of the network of highways throughout the land is essential. It would make no sense at all to abandon the highways and decide they can be junked like an old jalopy.
Okay, so we do need our highway system, and we want it to be useable. Cars and trucks ought to be able to traverse the highways. This includes not having to encounter gaping holes or drive across bridges that seem ready to collapse. This includes a relatively smooth ride that won’t bust your axel or pop your tires. This includes a clear indication of where the lanes are and indications about how to safely navigate the roadways.
Does that seem too much to ask?
Some want us to go further and undertake a futuristic upgrade of our highways. I’ll discuss this ambition more so in a moment. Right now, let’s merely focus on ensuring that the highways are sensibly fixed up and made safe enough that we can drive them without undue worries. In other words, putting to the side for a brief moment the advanced stuff, we ought to make sure that the basic blocking and tackling is being undertaken, if you get my drift.
There is a cost to getting the highways system back into shape, along with potentially furthering its readiness for the future.
And that’s where those highway dollars come into play.
How much do we need to spend on our highways?
Hold your breath, it is estimated to be into the billions and possibly trillions of dollars.
You could say that any prudent discussion about this kind of big dollars spending ought to also include a discussion about what we will get from those expenditures. That’s a topic I’ve previously discussed, see my coverage at this link here. Essentially, what is the ROI (return on investment) for the infrastructure bucks that are to be spent?
This brings us to the latest twist that is buzzing around.
In brief, our initial investment back in the 1950s through the 1970s was a first-time shot in the arm to our economic prowess. We gained a lot (most would reasonably agree, as mentioned earlier). This second booster shot is said to be less amorous in that it is not going to produce similar and pronounced long-term economic results.
Sure, there will be a lot of economic activity in the near term due to hiring taking place for roadway construction and while the infrastructure supply chain ramps up to revel in the spending. The qualm is that this is only a momentary boost and will not have a long-term effect per se. The crux to this argument is that we already derived the long-term bonuses by that initial investment of some many decades ago (a half-century, one might suggest).
Let’s ponder this.
Suppose you bought a product that helped you get into shape and would build your muscles and tone your body. You used the product for quite a while. Your body got into tremendous shape. Good for you.
The product though was wearing out over time. This meant that it was not doing quite as good a job at keeping you in a muscle-bound condition. The product still worked, fortunately, just not as best that it could. Worse still, the product might reach a point of injuring you, unintentionally so. The various mechanical parts and internal belts could snap at any time.
Each time that you use the product, you are now taking an increasingly heightened risk. On the one hand, the product was generally able to keep your body in shape. At the same time, there is a scary and mounting chance that the product might suddenly go haywire and you become harmed, doing so while simply trying to do what you’ve normally been doing with the product.
For various reasons, your only choice is to fix up the product, rather than replacing it outright.
The money that you spend to fix it is now going to aid in keeping your already toned body in ongoing shape for a while ahead. When you originally bought the product, it took you from being a weakling to the muscular specimen you are today. That was already accomplished. As such, this new investment is just going to keep things as they are.
That could be a disappointment if you were thinking that somehow the new investment was going to entirely remake your body. Nope, it is an investment that will keep you going, but not provide outsized or outstretched results.
The genie was already let out of the bottle. Those grand results are now under the bridge, in the sense that they were already incurred.
Are you going to be happy with this new investment?
It depends. If you expect that the investment is going to pretty much keep things at status quo, you presumably are satisfied with what the result is going to likely be. On the other hand, if you believe that the investment is going to have massive and heretofore unrealized gains, you are heading toward some quite sour disappointment.
This is the same sentiment generally being expressed by some about the new proposed investments in our highway system. The highway dollars are going to produce some temporary and near-term economic benefits, plus keep things going. This will also avert the dangers of injurious conditions that otherwise the highways were decaying into. Those are all dandy.
Anyone expecting that we will then see an economic boost to productivity or other societal factors are going to find themselves staring at a barren cupboard, some pundits proclaim. In a nutshell, we have presumably already reaped the mainstay of the benefits associated with a highway system. Seems like we are saddled with having to make the new investments for the sake of keeping things going. The icing on the cake is that short-term economic spike from highway construction activity.
Sad face.
We should always though be cautious about predicting the future.
I say this because many famous predictions have been made that were based on the prevailing conditions at the time of the prediction being fostered. You might recall various infamous predictions that the worldwide market for computers would only necessitate having to provide a handful of computers (in the days of those bulky and multi-ton hefty mainframes), or that there wasn’t any reason for someone to have a computer in their home (during the minicomputers era), or that 640KB should be enough for anyone to have in their computer (early days of microcomputers).
Those were seemingly sensible at the time they were stated. The prevailing mindset at the time of those predictions was ostensibly calibrated and guided by what was generally known and understood at that particular point in time.
Similarly, you might know that there is a fascinating debate about the use of horses in the early days of the automobile. Horses as a form of transport were the norm. Cars were just beginning to emerge. Some historical accounts indicate some people insisted that the horse was there to stay and the automobile was nothing more than a passing fad or quirky novelty. Supposedly, if you asked people what they wanted, they would have clamored for faster horses rather than seeking to have cars further embellished and made widely useable.
Again, this makes indubitable sense if you put yourself into the shoes of those living at that time. You see what you see, and make your predictions accordingly. It is easy to therefore not see what you cannot yet see. That’s a bit of a tongue twister. The point is that you tend to make assumptions shaped on whatever you have in hand.
Speaking of cars, the future of cars consists of AI-based true self-driving cars.
There isn’t a human driver involved in a true self-driving car. Keep in mind that true self-driving cars are driven via an AI driving system. There isn’t a need for a human driver at the wheel, and nor is there a provision for a human to drive the vehicle. For my extensive and ongoing coverage of Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) and especially self-driving cars, see the link here.
Here’s an intriguing question that is worth pondering: Could the advent of AI-based true self-driving cars be a heretofore missing and vital ingredient toward predicting the future benefits of having a viably maintained highway system?
Before jumping into the details, I’d like to further clarify what is meant when I refer to true self-driving cars.
Understanding The Levels Of Self-Driving Cars
As a clarification, true self-driving cars are ones that the AI drives the car entirely on its own and there isn’t any human assistance during the driving task.
These driverless vehicles are considered Level 4 and Level 5 (see my explanation at this link here), while a car that requires a human driver to co-share the driving effort is usually considered at Level 2 or Level 3. The cars that co-share the driving task are described as being semi-autonomous, and typically contain a variety of automated add-on’s that are referred to as ADAS (Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems).
There is not yet a true self-driving car at Level 5, which we don’t yet even know if this will be possible to achieve, and nor how long it will take to get there.
Meanwhile, the Level 4 efforts are gradually trying to get some traction by undergoing very narrow and selective public roadway trials, though there is controversy over whether this testing should be allowed per se (we are all life-or-death guinea pigs in an experiment taking place on our highways and byways, some contend, see my coverage at this link here).
Since semi-autonomous cars require a human driver, the adoption of those types of cars won’t be markedly different than driving conventional vehicles, so there’s not much new per se to cover about them on this topic (though, as you’ll see in a moment, the points next made are generally applicable).
For semi-autonomous cars, it is important that the public needs to be forewarned about a disturbing aspect that’s been arising lately, namely that despite those human drivers that keep posting videos of themselves falling asleep at the wheel of a Level 2 or Level 3 car, we all need to avoid being misled into believing that the driver can take away their attention from the driving task while driving a semi-autonomous car.
You are the responsible party for the driving actions of the vehicle, regardless of how much automation might be tossed into a Level 2 or Level 3.
Self-Driving Cars And Our Highway System
For Level 4 and Level 5 true self-driving vehicles, there won’t be a human driver involved in the driving task.
All occupants will be passengers.
The AI is doing the driving.
One aspect to immediately discuss entails the fact that the AI involved in today’s AI driving systems is not sentient. In other words, the AI is altogether a collective of computer-based programming and algorithms, and most assuredly not able to reason in the same manner that humans can.
Why this added emphasis about the AI not being sentient?
Because I want to underscore that when discussing the role of the AI driving system, I am not ascribing human qualities to the AI. Please be aware that there is an ongoing and dangerous tendency these days to anthropomorphize AI. In essence, people are assigning human-like sentience to today’s AI, despite the undeniable and inarguable fact that no such AI exists as yet.
With that clarification, you can envision that the AI driving system won’t natively somehow “know” about the facets of driving. Driving and all that it entails will need to be programmed as part of the hardware and software of the self-driving car.
Let’s dive into the myriad of aspects that come to play on this topic.
The question to be considered is somewhat straightforward.
Could the advent of AI-based true self-driving cars alter our prevailing viewpoint about predicting the benefits that will be accrued from investing in our highway system?
The answer is somewhat complicated, though decidedly worthwhile to give due consideration.
My short answer is that yes, I believe there is a basis and substantive value in incorporating the emergence of AI driving systems and self-driving autonomous vehicles into the calculations and equations used to make predictions about the payback from investments in an ongoing functional national highway system.
If you look at many of the economic models used to predict the impacts of new investments in our highways, they usually assume that cars are cars and that trucks are trucks. This means that cars are being driven by humans and that trucks are also being driven by humans.
Boldly, reconsider those fundamental and altogether crucial assumptions. Suppose there were AI driving systems that could sufficiently drive cars and do so without any human driver at the wheel. Assume the same about trucks.
Human drivers are relatively expensive. They are human labor and we have seen repeatedly that automation can typically perform the equivalent tasks at a much-lowered cost. Of course, let’s make clear, there are numerous exceptions to this rule. Especially if the task required employs human judgment or human skills that are not readily automatable.
In a manner of thinking, you could certainly question whether AI driving systems will rise to the level of human driving that is sufficient to replace the human labor used for driving purposes. We don’t yet know (see my detailed elaboration at this link here).
The existing tryouts are very narrow in their scope. It could be that we can make no further progress and end up with self-driving that only works in extremely constrained circumstances, such as at slow speeds in areas set aside for self-driving vehicles. Though that alone is beneficial, it isn’t the wide-scope hoped-for autonomous vehicle world that some enthusiastically envision.
Go with me for the moment and assume that we will achieve self-driving cars and self-driving trucks, doing so to the degree that the AI driving systems are able to drive (at least) on par with that of human drivers.
This ought to change how predictions are being made on the related economic benefits of a functioning highway system. Word to the wise: Remove from the traditional models those integral portions that are based on human-driven cars and human-driven trucks, and redo the modeling with autonomous vehicles such as self-driving cars and self-driving trucks.
This might require a significant overhaul of those prior models.
I say this because when I mention the notion of replacing one for the other, this has to be done sensibly. Those that merely plug in self-driving vehicles as though there is nothing different about them, other than lacking a human driver, are woefully under gauging the impacts of having self-driving among us.
There will be a sizable impact in many ways, including the legendary amplification of induced demand.
Induced demand consists of essentially unleashing hidden demand that comes out of the woodwork once something is more easily available or accessible. We’ve all undoubtedly experienced what happens when a new lane is added to a highway. Pretty soon, the new highway starts to get as swamped as did the other lanes of traffic. In the case of self-driving cars, many pundits predict that we will find ourselves entering into an era of mobility-for-all. People that until now have been mobility disadvantaged or impinged will start making use of cars.
Overall, you can expect:
· More people will be using cars (i.e., self-driving cars spur demand)
· Many more trips will be undertaken (easier to get around)
· Trips will become longer and longer in distances traveled (easier to travel afar)
Long-distance travel will especially blossom.
Much of the focus on the benefits of self-driving cars tend to concentrate on driving around town or within the confines of a city. That’s the mindset that goes along with labeling self-driving cars as robo-taxis. We only consider taxis to be an around-town kind of contrivance. You might recall those humorous scenes in movies and TV shows that used to make a joke about someone taking a taxi to get from one city to the next, or utterly ridiculing the notion of using a taxi to get from one state to another state in the US.
Heaven forbid, nobody would do such a thing.
Time to toss out that mislabeling.
People are likely to utilize self-driving cars for all types of long-distance travel.
For example, you get up in the morning at your rural home and use a self-driving car to drive you downtown as part of your daily work commute. Whereas you used to have to be the driver, contending with all the usual driving frustrations, and be fully alert and awake as you do so, the self-driving car allows you to catch some extra sleep on the way to the office. Assume that’s about a one-to-two-hour daily commute, each way.
You have friends that live in a city that is many miles away from where you live. Driving to go see them is always a pain since you had to make that exhausting drive. Via a self-driving car, you can joyfully make the journey. While inside the self-driving car, you can bring up some online videos or movies on the interior LED displays and leisurely count the time it takes to get to your friend's place. Assume that’s a two-to-three-hour drive, each way.
As a keystone heads-up, I’ve explained in prior columns that the widespread advent of self-driving cars will likely alter our cultural perception of distance and time, see the analysis at this link here. In case that seems rather inflated, consider what happened when we transitioned from horses to the use of automobiles. The perception of long distances tended to shrink in the sense that you could go much longer distances in a relatively shorter period of time. This same reorientation will occur due to the prevalence of self-driving cars.
Follow me on this with some quick examples.
Suppose you are living in Los Angeles. Pretend the weekend is coming up and you want to drive to Las Vegas, Nevada. That is about a 270-mile drive and can be quite boring since it is primarily a traversal through desert highways. Via a self-driving car, and still going at the legal speed limits, the otherwise four or maybe five-hour drive can whisk you to Vegas while you are snoozing or watching films (maybe about gambling and how to win at the poker table).
Okay, we’ve now gotten ourselves readily taking a five-hour driving journey, but without having to do any driving since the AI driving system is handling it all for you.
There’s more.
Some relatives of yours are living in Phoenix, Arizona, and are those proverbial snowbirds (people that come to Phoenix during the winter from other colder climates as a means of escaping the freezing snow and ice). You would relish going to see them but the drive from Los Angeles is about six or seven hours long.
No problem with a self-driving car.
After work on a Friday night, you get into a self-driving car and by the time morning arises, you’ve arrived in Phoenix. Unlike trying to fly there, you didn’t have to go to a packed airport, you didn’t have to sit in an airplane with a bunch of impatient and irritating fellow flyers, etc. You enjoyed the personal comforts of a private and quiet car ride.
Think about all the changes that will occur regarding the expanded view about:
· Visiting of friends
· Visiting of relatives
· Leisure or vacation trips
· Commuting to work
· Attending conferences
· Business trips
· Etc.
That’s why you cannot simply take a model that has conventional cars as the mode of transit and in any perfunctory way swap out those cars for instead the use of self-driving cars.
A paradigm shift is required.
The impact will occur for trips:
· Within and across a town or city
· Within and across a region
· Within and across a state (intrastate travel)
· Amongst and across states (interstate travel)
· Among and across countries (e.g., USA, Mexico, Canada)
The national highway system is the interconnecting piece to all of this.
Without the nationwide highway system up to par and being in decent shape, you would only end up with localized benefits of self-driving cars. Essentially, the self-driving car usage would be confined to primarily local kinds of travel and not readily be able to make those fuller long-distance trips.
There is a well-known computational model that covers long-distance travel and was devised via the support of the U.S. Department of Transportation and the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA). Known commonly as the rJourney model, it has no official provision as yet for the inclusion of self-driving cars and nor self-driving trucks. Researchers have been leveraging the model to see if it can be retrofitted or potentially revamped accordingly.
Here’s what the DOT had originally indicated about the model (which was initially based on travel data from 2010): “The US Department of Transportation (US DOT) recognizes that long-distance travel represents a significant portion of all travel and that this type of travel is economically important. In 1995, the date of the last long-distance passenger travel survey in the United States, 25% of all person-miles traveled in the United States were classified as long-distance travel. Long-distance travel includes both Business and Leisure travel, both of which are major contributors to the United States economy. As a result, the US DOT desires to support continued high levels of personal mobility for both economic and social purposes.”
This clearly showcases the logical and altogether sensible assertion that our travel has substantive impacts economically. Therefore, if our travel habits and tendencies are going to dramatically be reshaped due to the use of self-driving cars, it stands to reason that we are bound to experience notable economic differences.
It’s time to figure those out.
Conclusion
There are a lot more twists and turns on this topic.
For example, as earlier intimated, some argue we need to ensure that the highway dollars go toward adding all sorts of high-tech to our roadway infrastructure. I’ve addressed those points in my prior column postings, see the link here.
In short, the question arises as to how much of the money should go toward fixing the highway system so that it is passable by human driver standards versus doing presumed upgrades or advancements that will further enable the use of autonomous vehicles.
One fervent posture is that the funds ought to be used to make things easier for self-driving cars and self-driving trucks to traverse our highways. Not everyone concurs about that perspective, especially if this implies that there is somehow less done toward ensuring that human drivers are able to sufficiently traverse our national highways.
At least that recognizes the importance of thinking about autonomous vehicles.
The main gripe surfaced in this discussion is that numerous modelers and pontificators about the highway system are seemingly ignoring the potential emergence of self-driving vehicles all told. They aren’t even downplaying the impact, and instead are omitting it mindlessly (out of sight, out of mind).
I realize it is hard right now to envision a nation that is being continually traversed by self-driving cars. Notice too that I didn’t even bring up the notion of empty self-driving cars, ones that are making a road trip and there isn’t any human inside the autonomous vehicle. This is another use of self-driving cars that we have to encompass into our models.
If we look back at history and recalibrate those early predictions associated with computers, we know now that the world did indeed need more than just a handful of computers, and that we do have computers generally in every home, and that we surely needed more than just 640K bytes of memory for our computers.
Do this: Turn the clock forward toward the near future.
Let’s please not be chagrined and upon belated reflection have a dismal sinking feeling or abject realization that we blatantly forgot to consider the role of self-driving vehicles. That’s a “missing factor” that will leave us ill-prepared and decidedly ridiculed by an endless stream of stinging and satirical memes, or worse.
That will be gosh-darned hard to stomach and a pitiful shame.
